pages.title: Studio
pages.content:
Form & Fjord was founded in 2014 by two graphic designers and an architect who shared a desk and an opinion: that good design is mostly careful listening, followed by doing less.

Today we are six people in a former print workshop by the water. We take on a small number of projects each year and stay with them for a long time, often for a decade or more.

How we work

  1. We start every project on site, never from a brief alone.
  2. We test with real people at full size.
  3. We write the manual ourselves and keep it short.
  4. We stay available after launch.

Clarity is a form of kindness.

Studio principle N°1

pages.title: Approach
pages.content:
Our process has four steps, and we show our clients every one of them. There are no big reveals: the work grows in the open.

Fees are fixed per phase, agreed before we start each one.

posts.title: Kunsthalle Vestre
posts.excerpt: A flexible identity for a small art hall: three shapes, three colours and a typographic system that bends to every exhibition.
posts.content:
Kunsthalle Vestre shows six exhibitions a year with a team of five. The old identity needed a designer for every poster. The new one had to be something the team could run themselves, without losing its character.

Three shapes, one grid

We reduced the identity to a circle, a triangle and a stack of bars, each tied to one of the hall's programme strands: light, mass and rhythm. Every poster places one shape on the same twelve-column grid, and the exhibition title always sits at the bottom left.

  • A poster template for print and screens
  • A typographic system with two weights
  • Signage for the entrance and the courtyard
  • A short manual the staff actually read

Two years on, the hall has produced over forty posters in-house. None of them look the same, and all of them look like Vestre.

For the first time, the posters feel like part of the building.

Director, Kunsthalle Vestre

comments.author: Liv
comments.content: The poster system is a lesson in restraint. Lovely to see it working two years later.

comments.author: Jonas
comments.content: Is the manual available to read anywhere?

posts.title: Harbour Line Wayfinding
posts.excerpt: Signage for a ferry terminal used by twelve thousand people a day, most of them in a hurry.
posts.content:
The Harbour Line terminal connects trains, trams and three ferry routes under one long roof. Travellers have about ninety seconds to make a decision. Our job was to make that decision obvious.

We started with a walk-through at rush hour, timing how long people stood still at each junction. The worst spots were not where signs were missing but where too many signs competed.

Fewer, larger, closer

We removed half of the existing signs and made the rest larger, placing them exactly where the decision happens rather than where a wall happened to be free.

Gates got single letters in coloured circles. Platforms got numbers you can read from forty metres. Everything else became secondary information in a smaller size.

Average standing time at the main junction dropped from eleven seconds to four.

comments.author: Mette
comments.content: Four seconds instead of eleven. That is the best design metric I have read this year.

posts.title: Nord Grotesk
posts.excerpt: A workhorse grotesk in six weights, drawn for signage first and books second.
posts.content:
Nord Grotesk began as lettering for the Harbour Line signs and grew into a full family. Its proportions come from the sign panels: slightly narrow, generous counters, and an uppercase that holds up at a distance.

We drew six weights, from light to extra bold, and kept the spacing loose enough for small sizes. The figures are tabular by default because so much of public information is numbers: platforms, times, gates.

Design notes

  • A single-storey g for clarity at small sizes
  • Short descenders so tight line spacing works on signs
  • An arrow set drawn to match every weight

The family is now used across all of our wayfinding projects and is available to clients under a studio licence.

posts.title: Regional Transit Diagram
posts.excerpt: Four lines, forty stations and one rule: every angle is forty-five degrees.
posts.content:
The regional transport authority asked for a map that would fit on a bus shelter panel and still make sense to a first-time visitor. Geography had to give way to clarity.

We simplified the network into straight runs and forty-five degree turns, kept the four line colours from the existing fleet and gave every interchange the same white circle with a heavy outline.

The diagram was tested with groups of commuters and tourists before printing. Two stations moved, one name became shorter and the yellow got slightly darker so it would print reliably outdoors.

posts.title: Four Seasons of Sound
posts.excerpt: A season of concerts announced with four posters that share nothing but a grid and a number.
posts.content:
A concert hall wanted a season campaign that would read from across a tram platform. We proposed four posters, one per quarter, each built from stripes or a single circle.

The posters carry almost no text: the season number, the dates and a short address line. Everything else lives online. The restraint made the street posters feel like objects rather than adverts.

Printed in two spot colours on uncoated paper, the series was later collected into a small folded edition for subscribers.

posts.title: Stol N°3
posts.excerpt: A stacking chair for a library reading room, in ash and powder-coated steel.
posts.content:
The library needed eighty chairs that could be stacked by one person, survive school groups and look calm in a room full of books. We designed one chair and changed it eleven times.

The final version uses a steel frame with an ash seat and a single coloured backrest. The red backrest became the library's own signal colour, repeated in the shelf labels.

A small workshop outside the city builds the chairs to order. Every one carries a stamped number under the seat.

posts.title: Index: A Book on Nordic Modernism
posts.excerpt: A 320-page survey designed around its index, which turned out to be the best part of the book.
posts.content:
The editors had collected two hundred buildings, chairs, posters and teaspoons. The challenge was to let a reader move through them in any order without getting lost.

We built the book around the index. Every object has a number, the number appears in the margin on every page that mentions it, and full-page colour plates break the text at regular intervals.

  • 320 pages, sewn binding, open flat
  • Two paper stocks: uncoated text, coated plates
  • Set in Nord Grotesk and a mono for references

The first printing sold out in four months. The second added a fold-out timeline at the back, requested by almost every reader who wrote to us.

posts.title: Fjord Housing Annual Review
posts.excerpt: A housing trust's year told in numbers, with one colour reserved for good news.
posts.content:
Annual reports are usually written for the board. Fjord Housing wanted one their tenants would read. We kept it short, put the numbers first and used red only where something had improved.

Charts are drawn on the same grid as the text so a bar chart and a paragraph can share a spread without fighting. Photographs of the buildings were replaced by simple drawings of their facades.

The review was printed as a newspaper and delivered to every flat. Response forms came back at three times the usual rate.
